venue_now: arXiv 2603.02239 (the fetched PDF, per MANIFEST.json); the text carries no venue header and no arXiv stamp, so the catalogue's Computers & Industrial Engineering 2026 (doi:10.1016/j.cie.2026.112333) is not confirmed by the file
what_it_is: ERI is a taxonomy-driven instruction dataset for training and evaluating engineering LLMs: 57,750 instruction-response records over nine engineering fields, 55 subdomains, seven intent types (definition, explanation, calculation, comparison, design, troubleshooting, code) and three difficulty tiers (undergraduate, graduate, professional), 50 records per cell (p.1, p.5, p.7). Every record, reference response included, was written by an LLM (GPT-5 Mini) from a (field, subdomain, intent, tier) seed, five pairs per API call and ten calls per cell, then schema-checked, deduplicated and length-filtered, with a GPT-5.1 quality rating on a random 10% (p.9, p.12, p.18). Seven models were evaluated on a stratified 10% subset of over 5,000 items: three LLM judges from different providers each gave a holistic 1-5 score against the model-written reference, and the three scores were averaged (p.13-14). In place of human verification, a 'convergent validation' argument from cross-model agreement is offered to bound hallucinated references at 1.7% of items (p.18).
domain: engineering: civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, environmental, aerospace, materials, industrial, fire science (p.1, p.6)
size: 57,750 records generated (p.1, p.5); released splits of 45,415 train, 2,671 validation and 5,343 test records (p.22); 7 models evaluated on a stratified 10% subset (over 5,000 items), 115,962 judgments (p.13-14)
source_of_items: generated by an LLM (GPT-5 Mini) from (field, subdomain, intent, difficulty) seeds; the reference responses are model-written too (p.9, p.18)
instances: static: generated once by an LLM and released as fixed JSONL splits; no variants, no regeneration (p.9, p.22)
has_gold_traces: no: each record has a model-written free-text reference response; the calculation intent's success criterion asks responses to 'present key steps for auditability' (p.7), but no intermediate value is verified or scored
evaluation: LLM judge: a holistic 1-5 score from each of three judges (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Mistral Small 3) given the question, the reference answer and the response, averaged (p.14). The paper also describes automatic checks (empty output, refusal, missing final answer, a constraint-satisfaction flag where bounds parse, numeric and unit extraction on the calculation subset) and an eight-letter rubric checklist (p.8-9, p.12-13), but the reported study uses only the averaged judge score.
human_validation: None. Only inter-judge agreement is reported: Spearman 0.70 to 0.80 between judge pairs, within-one-point agreement above 85% (p.14). The 'convergent validity' analysis (the three frontier models all score at least 4.0 on 68.8% of items; 1.7% of items have frontier scores of 3.0 or below; score inversions under 0.1%) is offered as a bound on hallucinated references (p.18). Expert validation of a stratified subsample and a human-verified gold subset are named as future work (p.18, p.20).
contamination_measures: none: the records are public on GitHub and Hugging Face, with a training split (p.1, p.22); exact and optional semantic deduplication target redundancy, not contamination (p.12)

engtrace_use.explanation: Belongs in: the engineering paragraph. Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It is the broadest multi-field engineering benchmark found, its nine fields include all five EngTrace branches (p.6), and it cites EngTrace's arXiv version as reference [29] (p.9, p.25). It bears on the May sentence that generalist suites 'restrict assessment to factual recall via multiple-choice questions' (May p.2): ERI is open-ended, but scored by LLM judges against LLM-written references.

suggested_wording: ERI (Naser et al., 2026) covers nine engineering fields and three difficulty tiers with 57,750 instruction-response records written by an LLM, and scores responses with three LLM judges against those model-written references, without human verification of references or judges.

overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-branch engineering scope (its nine fields include civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical and industrial engineering, all five EngTrace branches, p.6), difficulty tiers (p.1) and synthetic generation (p.9). Lacks: answers or intermediate values computed by code (the references are GPT-5 Mini text, p.18); gold traces; step-level or deterministic scoring in the reported study (one holistic judge score, p.14); any human validation of items or evaluator (p.18); contamination control (public splits including a training split, p.22). What EngTrace adds: instances and gold solutions computed by template code; deterministic answer, milestone and per-claim arithmetic checks, with an LLM judge only for milestones those checks miss, validated against labels from 15 experts (X1: 300 traces); certification of every template by three own-branch experts; and a pool drawn from a private seed.
notes: (1) ERI cites EngTrace (ref. [29], arXiv 2511.01650, p.25) as support for LLM-generated data: 'The recent EngTrace benchmark explicitly makes this argument, noting that its "entirely synthetic" dataset enables controlled evaluation' (p.9). EngTrace's synthetic items are generated by code with computed answers, unlike ERI's LLM-written records; the revision may want to draw that distinction. (2) The file is the arXiv version: no journal header, no arXiv stamp; the C&IE venue in the catalogue is not confirmed by the text. (3) Internal inconsistencies: the conclusion calls it the 'Engineering Reasoning and Intelligence (ERI)' benchmark (p.21); the data-availability note says 'available on request' (p.22) while the dataset is linked publicly (p.1, p.22); the listed splits total 53,429 records (p.22) against 57,750 generated (p.5), a gap the paper does not explain. (4) The claim that reference errors 'affect all models equally and therefore do not distort rankings' (p.18) is asserted, not shown. (5) The search note's description (nine fields, 57,750 records, judge panel, 1.7% bound, cites EngTrace) matches the text.
